title: What's a Distraction? (Woodenization Example)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. lays out a compact, three-step "Woodenization" mini-lesson for directly teaching students what a distraction actually is, designed to fill just 10-15 minutes of class time once a year. Step one has students engage in provisional writing on prompts like "What's a distraction? Give an example," aiming for about 100 words in 5-10 minutes; step two moves them into brief pair or small-group discussion via his Conversation Challenge protocol; step three brings the class to a shared working definition modeled on Chris Bailey's Hyperfocus: "a distraction is anything that hinders you from accomplishing your goal or task." He illustrates the definition with two contrasting scenarios — studying versus hanging out with friends — to show that what counts as a distraction is context-dependent, then closes with two practical tips: putting the phone away and writing down nagging thoughts on an index card. Stuart frames the whole exercise as unusually efficient motivational work, arguing it simultaneously boosts the Effort, Efficacy, Credibility, and Belonging beliefs from his Five Key Beliefs framework despite its brevity.
points: The mini-lesson follows a tight three-step structure — provisional writing, brief paired discussion, whole-class definition-building — designed to fit inside 10-15 minutes of class time.

Stuart anchors the class's working definition in Chris Bailey's Hyperfocus ("a distraction is anything that hinders you from accomplishing your goal or task"), giving students language rather than just a vague warning.
Contrasting the studying scenario with the hanging-out-with-friends scenario makes the point that the same input can be a distraction in one context and not another.
His two practical takeaways — put the phone away, write nagging thoughts on an index card — give students concrete tools rather than leaving the discussion purely conceptual.
He explicitly credits this brief mini-lesson with boosting four of his Five Key Beliefs simultaneously (Effort, Efficacy, Credibility, Belonging), arguing brevity doesn't limit motivational payoff.
quotes: This is actually a great question to spend 10-15 minutes of class time on at least once per school year.
I like to get my students writing for up to 5-10 minutes, aiming at producing 100 words (roughly half of a lined sheet of paper).
A distraction is anything that hinders you from accomplishing your goal or task.

If you're trying to study, a distraction could be your phone, your little sibling, or your wandering thoughts about friends. If you're trying to enjoy time hanging out with your friends, a distraction could be your phone or your wandering thoughts about schoolwork.

Woodenization mini-lessons like this are super productive for student motivation in that they clarify good effort (Effort belief booster), make the path to success clearer (Efficacy booster), demonstrate that I'm a capable teacher (Credibility booster), and signal that all students get distracted (Belonging booster).
